beneficiaries_note: Founds charities: each charity it launched, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: Ambitious Impact (formerly Charity Entrepreneurship) researches intervention ideas and founds new charities to run the best of them; this model covers all its programmes in the year to March 2025: the nine charities and five effective giving organisations it launched, Founding to Give, its funding circles, grantmaker and research training, and its research, against its own spending of $2.5M (the $2.5M of seed grants it passed on are the new charities' money). At the defaults it averts about 20 years of healthy life per $1,000: each organisation founded is credited with the average lifetime fundraising of its charities ($107M raised by 60 so far, times 2.5 for the years to come), half of it caused by Ambitious Impact, valued at the figures the rankings give the charities it has launched, half counted as new money, the next dollar at 36% of the past average. It is more than ten times its peers because it creates charities that each go on to raise and spend several times its cost per charity, most of them in global health near the cause's average: it sits above the charities it founds, not among typical global-health programmes. The result moves most with the next-dollar figure, the discount rate, how much its charities will raise over their lives and how much of their existence it caused; the spending its grantmaker training and research changed and its fellows' careers are discounted for missing data.

resources.title: Charity Entrepreneurship (Ambitious Impact), charity 1195850, Trustees' Report and Audited Financial Statements, year ended 31 March 2025 (Moore Kingston Smith LLP; filed copy of the Charity Commission's register)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Charities it has launched since 2018
rows.explainer: Its own count, "60+": 60 as stated (more would lower the average a little). Includes those that have closed, so the average below counts failures.

rows.label: Money raised so far per charity launched, failures included (US$)
rows.explainer: About $1.8M per charity: an average over every cohort since 2018, the ones that closed and the young ones that have barely started included.

rows.label: A launched charity's lifetime fundraising as a multiple of the average raised so far
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The average so far stops at today: the charities are on average about three years old (cohorts of 6 to 10 a year since 2018, most of them since 2021), and the ones that survive grow (Fortify Health, Suvita, Family Empowerment Media, Shrimp Welfare Project and Ansh now spend $1M to $5M a year; GiveWell has funded 13). A charity's whole life raises more than its first three years: 2.5 times (1.5 if most of the money comes from a few charities whose growth has peaked, 5 if the survivors keep growing for a decade, as Fortify Health has since 2018). Closures are in the multiple: the failed ones add nothing further.

rows.label: Years from launch to the middle of a charity's lifetime spending
rows.explainer: Our judgment. A charity raises little in its first year (a seed grant of $150,000 to $190,000) and more as it scales, so half its lifetime money is spent about four years after launch (two if it stays small, seven if it grows for a decade).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the charities spend the money
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: An effective giving organisation's lifetime spending as a share of an incubated charity's
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The five are new national giving platforms, typically run by one or two staff and volunteers, against an incubated charity's $0.2M to $2M: 30% (10% to 80%). What they spend is valued at the charities their donors fund, through the destinations below; their own leverage (money moved per dollar) isn't credited, so no money is counted twice.

rows.label: Share of each founded organisation's existence Ambitious Impact caused
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Without the programme some of these organisations would exist anyway, later or in another form: founders who would have started a charity on their own, ideas others were already pursuing (lead paint, tobacco taxes, kangaroo care), funders who would have backed the same team. And the founders give up other good work (their alternative careers at effective organisations), which this share also nets out. Half (25% to 80%). Anchors: AIM picks the idea, recruits and trains the founders, pairs them and finds the seed money (about 95% of proposals funded); against that, the site's own-effect share for money a meta charity records is 30% (15% to 45%, @meta.own_effect_share), and a founder's alternative career counts against it.

rows.label: Money the organisations it founded in the year will raise and spend, caused by it, discounted (US$)
rows.formula: (ceip_charities_launched + egi_orgs_launched * egi_spend_vs_charity) * raised_per_charity_to_date * lifetime_vs_to_date * spend_wait_discount * aim_share_of_founding
rows.explainer: The year's new organisations, each at the average charity's lifetime fundraising (raised so far × the lifetime multiple, closures included), discounted for the wait, times Ambitious Impact's share of their existence. This money is valued below as money moved: at the figures of the charities it founds, new money in full and shifted money only for its gain.

source.quote: training 14 grantmakers who collectively control approximately $40 million per year

rows.explainer: Grantmakers at foundations and family offices, trained in its programme in the year.

rows.label: Share of those grants its training moved to better uses, summed over the years it lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Most of a trained grantmaker's portfolio is set by the foundation's mandate; training changes how some grants are chosen (cost-effectiveness, evidence, neglected areas) for a few years. 4% of a year's grants (1% to 12%). Anchor: Ambitious Impact's own estimate of about $3M of counterfactual value from the cohort (p. 17), 7.5% of $40M, before any discount for its self-assessment; Rethink Priorities' research is credited 3% to 5% of the money it informs (our model of it).

rows.label: Money outside its own incubation its published research informs in a year (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Its research team recommended 12 ideas in the year (p. 10), with public reports and cost-effectiveness analyses. Most of that work feeds its own incubation (counted above, its cost in program_spend); others read it too: funders sizing grants to the new charities and to ideas others run, and other incubators and researchers. $5M a year informed ($1M to $20M), as for Rethink Priorities' surveys ($5M).

rows.label: Share of that money its research moved to better uses
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Rethink Priorities' cross-cause research (3%, 1% to 10%): a report sharpens or redirects a small part of the grants that read it.

rows.label: Spending its grantmaker training and research changed, in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Money informed × the share changed, for both. All shifted: these funders would have granted the money anyway, so it counts only for the gain over where it would have gone (informed_money_value). The money raised that it caused is in raised_money.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to the charities it founds (its charities on the rankings, live), units of value
rows.explainer: The charities it has launched that the site ranks, each at its figure on the rankings (its primary evaluator's: GiveWell for Suvita, Family Empowerment Media, Fortify Health, Ansh, Taimaka, Lafiya Nigeria, Notify Health, Healthy Futures Global, Clear Solutions and Spiro; the Happier Lives Institute for ACTRA; Ambitious Impact's own idea-stage estimates for the eleven young ones that have no other; Animal Charity Evaluators for Shrimp Welfare Project; Ambitious Impact for Animal Policy International), equal weights within each cause, and the two causes in the shares of the ideas its research recommended in the year (nine human, three animal). Its charities without a model here (LEEP, whose only model is unpublished, FarmKind, Rahi Impact, Scale Welfare, Radius, the Institute for Development Innovation and others) are valued at the average of their cause; its meta charities (CEARCH, Better Futures Guide) and the effective giving organisations at the average of the rest. Equal weights, not money weights: the charities that raised most (GiveWell's grantees) would weigh more by money, and they sit near the global-health average.

Side effects of founding charities beyond the money counted, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Good the branches leave out: founders trained who later lead other organisations, the ideas and open cost-effectiveness analyses other charities and governments use, new markets its charities open (stunning equipment, fortified flour) that others enter. Harm: staff time of governments and partners its failed charities used, and the closure of the weakest. Net +10% (0% to +30%).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's money went: its own published split, each recipient at its live result on this site (value_destinations).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: an ordinary charity of each cause its money goes to, in its own mix), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the shared rule for an organisation whose money goes to several causes. Shifted money would have gone to an ordinary charity of the same cause: each cause's at the rule for a mover in that cause (GiveDirectly's live result, times a shared multiple, 1×, from 0 to 3×, over the global-health charities' on the rankings, times that cause's charities'), weighted by the organisation's own split, all live under your values.

rows.label: Value of a dollar all shifted (given anyway, now to a better use), units of value
rows.explainer: Money that would have been given or spent anyway counts only for the gain over where it would have gone: a grantmaker's grants, or spending that research or advice changed.

rows.label: Value of the spending its research or advice changed (all shifted money), units of value
rows.explainer: Spending its research or advice changed, at a judged share of the money it informed: all of it would have been spent anyway, so it counts for the gain over where it would have gone, discounted for weak evidence and for an outcome not measured for this charity (docs/normalization.md 2.8, 2.12).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Value of the money it caused to be raised and the spending it changed (units of value)
rows.explainer: The money raised for its charities and through its circles and companies, net of where shifted money would have gone, plus the spending its training and research changed, all shifted, with its evidence and missing-data steps; then the side effects.

Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Applies to the spending its training and research changed (informed_money_value) and to the empty policy branch. Grantmaking training and research reports may move grants the wrong way as well as the right one, and its own estimate of the training's value is a self-assessment: 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), as for Rethink Priorities' cross-cause research.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what would have happened anyway is in each branch's own row (the share changed, the shared new-money share, its share of the founding).

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: 1: other contributors are in the branches (funders' money through the shared new-money share, founders' alternative work in aim_share_of_founding).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step for the spending its training and research changed: the money informed and the share changed are judgments, not counts. The money raised for its charities is counted (their fundraising, its own count) and takes no missing-data step, as for every meta charity's money moved; the careers have their own.

rows.label: All adjustments combined

rows.explainer: The policy branch is empty; the money raised and the spending changed count their own steps (moved_value), the fellows' careers theirs.
